canonicalExplanation.summary: An **object** groups named properties: `{ id: 7, title: "Loops" }`. Read with dot (`lesson.title`) or brackets (`lesson[key]`) when the name is in a variable. Use **property shorthand** (`{ id, title }`) and **optional chaining** (`lesson.author?.name`) to avoid crashes on missing parts. To ask whether a property belongs to the object itself, use `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` — the `in` operator also finds **inherited** properties from the prototype chain.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A settings loader checks `if ("toString" in userSettings)` to see if the user configured a "toString" option — and it's always true, even for an empty object! `in` looked up the prototype chain and found the built-in method. Object.hasOwn distinguishes an own configuration key from one inherited through the prototype chain. In this lesson you'll model and validate a small domain record with property shorthand and safe access.

```predict
{"question": "`const s = {}; console.log(\"toString\" in s, Object.hasOwn(s, \"toString\"));` Output?", "options": ["false false", "true false"], "answer": 1, "why": "`in` finds inherited properties (toString comes from Object.prototype). hasOwn checks only the object's own keys."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Control flow and functions** module, **Data-structure choice**, **let, const and binding**, and **Records and entities** (fields describing one entity).

sections.heading: The model: own properties, safe access, validation
sections.body:
```js
function makeLesson({ id, title, minutes = 10, author = null }) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(id) || id <= 0) throw new TypeError("id must be a positive integer");
  if (typeof title !== "string" || title.trim() === "") throw new TypeError("title is required");
  return { id, title: title.trim(), minutes, author };   // property shorthand.
}

const lesson = makeLesson({ id: 7, title: " Loops " });
lesson.title;                  // "Loops"
lesson.author?.name;           // undefined — no crash.
const key = "minutes";
lesson[key];                   // 10
Object.hasOwn(lesson, "id");   // true
Object.keys(lesson);           // ["id", "title", "minutes", "author"]
```

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| read a known name. | `obj.name`. |
| read a name in a variable. | `obj[key]`. |
| maybe-missing nested value. | `obj.a?.b`. |
| is it the object's own key? | `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)`. |
| list own keys. | `Object.keys(obj)`. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "What's the risk of `obj[userInput] = value` with arbitrary keys?", "answer": "Keys like \"__proto__\" can tamper with the prototype. For user-controlled keys, use a Map or `Object.create(null)`."}
```

examples.title: Own settings vs inherited ones
examples.situation: Object.hasOwn distinguishes an own configuration key from one inherited through the prototype chain.
walkthrough: **Bug:** `"toString" in userSettings` is true for `{}` because toString is inherited from Object.prototype.
**Own configuration key:** `Object.hasOwn(userSettings, "toString")` is false for `{}` and true only if the user set it.
**Validate:** the loader will read only own keys with `Object.keys(userSettings)` and reject unknown ones.
examples.result: The loader only treats keys the user actually set as configuration.

examples.title: The crash on a missing author
examples.situation: `lesson.author.name` throws "Cannot read properties of null" for lessons without an author.
walkthrough: author is null for some lessons.
examples.result: Lessons without an author display "Codestead team" instead of crashing.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The in operator checks only an object's own properties.
misconceptions.correction: in also returns true for properties inherited through the prototype chain, like toString. Object.hasOwn checks only the object's own properties.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why was "toString" in s true?

analogy.example: An object is like a **labelled drawer set**. `in` asks "is there a drawer with this label here or in the cupboard it came from?"; hasOwn asks "is there a drawer with this label in *this* set?".
limitations: Drawer sets don't inherit; objects do via prototypes.
Optional chaining is like checking the drawer exists before opening it.

steps.explanation: The user configured nothing, so there are no own keys.
in finds the key inherited through the prototype chain.
Object.hasOwn distinguishes an own configuration key from an inherited one.

trace.textAlternative: Own vs inherited properties. Step 1, Empty object: own keys is []. The user configured nothing, so there are no own keys. Step 2, in operator: 'toString' in settings is true (inherited). in finds the key inherited through the prototype chain. Step 3, hasOwn: Object.hasOwn is false. Object.hasOwn distinguishes an own configuration key from an inherited one.

remediation.explanation: For each property access ask: **Could this be missing? → ?. and ??. Is the key from a variable? → brackets. Do I mean own properties? → Object.hasOwn.**

recap.summary: To model and validate a small domain record, build it with shorthand and defaults, validate types at creation, read with dot, brackets or optional chaining, and use Object.hasOwn — not in — to check the object's own properties.
